newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Freedom at issue on eve of Hong Kong handover.
newsitem.headline: Freedom at issue on eve of Hong Kong handover.

text.p: On the eve of Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule, the departing British colonialists on Sunday vowed to defend its democracy, but Beijing's handpicked future leader insisted freedom would have limits.
Outgoing Governor Chris Patten attacked "demeaning, patronising, mule headed" arguments against democracy.
But future chief executive Tung Chee-hwa defended a decision to ban protests attacking Chinese leaders and advocating independence for Taiwan and Tibet.

Amid festivity on the streets, decked with the bauhinia flower flags of the new Hong Kong, tensions that have bedevilled the British retreat focused on political arrangements after the transition at midnight (1600 GMT) on Monday.

Having chided Beijing over its decision to assert its sovereignty by swiftly sending in 4,000 troops, armoured vehicles, helicopters and warships, Britain's Foreign Secretary said London would keep China to its promise to hold popular elections within a year.
"The people of Hong Kong have now had a taste of democracy. It must be a prime objective of British policy to make sure that taste does not become a memory," Robin Cook told reporters.

But in a radio interview, incoming chief executive Tung Chee-hwa said while he had no objection to protesters burning his effigy, attacks on Beijing leaders and advocacy of independence for Taiwan and Tibet would be another matter.

To avoid any risk of encountering demonstrators, Chinese President Jiang Zemin and Premier Li Peng are due to sail across Victoria Harbour to Hong Kong island late on Monday to receive the territory back from Britain's Prince Charles.

Tung has warned pro-democracy activists against staging a protest on the balcony of the legislature building in the first few hours of Chinese rule while Beijing-appointed lawmakers were being sworn in.
Under controversial laws prepared by the new legislature and due to come into force at midnight, people will need police approval to stage protests.
Cook said he pressed Tung when they met aboard the British royal yacht Britannia on Saturday to ensure that "elections should not just be held, but be held on a free and fair basis".
Tung promised a vote within a year, and Cook said Britain would draw on international support to ensure the pledge was kept.

After Monday night's handover ceremonies, Cook and Prime Minister Tony Blair will boycott the swearing-in of the new legislature that replaces a popularly-elected body. It has been meeting unofficially in China so far.
Patten lambasted "that small band of self-appointed good-mouthers who tell the world that Hong Kongers don't care about democracy and civil liberties but only about making money".
In a radio address, he said demonstrators who take to the streets each June 4 to mark the anniversary of the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre in Beijing "gave an eloquent answer to that nonsense".
Patten's crusade for free elections in Hong Kong plunged relations between Britain and China into crisis. A furious Beijing called him a "whore".
The political row was forgotton or ignored by Hong Kong residents on Sunday, as a bright sun illuminated the twilight of imperial rule.
It was a harbinger of hope for superstitious Hong Kongers, though weather experts said the typhoon season might yet dump rain on the final parades and flourishes on Monday.

Chinese families posed for pictures in front of the Britannia, moored on the Victoria Harbour waterfront, and outside Government House, where Britain's royal coat of arms will soon be removed from the gates.
The red five-star Chinese flag was unfurled a little bit ahead of time by several junks plying the choppy waters of the harbour.

Tourists formed long queues to board a tram that climbs almost vertically up Victoria Peak, which commands spectacular views over what was once a "barren rock" and is now a glittering city of 6.4 million.

Inside the gilded ballroom of Government House, Britain's heir to the throne Prince Charles, in naval tropical whites, performed one of the last rites of empire, handing out 116 knighthoods and other honours.
Across the border, the Chinese city of Shenzhen was festooned with red lanterns and banners welcoming the return of Hong Kong after 156 years of British colonial rule.
Beijing also was in carnival mood with tens of thousands of people clogging streets into the small hours of Sunday.
Many sat on street corners, playing cards, chatting excitedly and revelling in a transition that will expunge a century and a half of colonial humilitation.
